reference.source: Inherited arrhythmia and cardiac electrophysiology references
clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function variants in KCNH2 (hERG, Kv11.1), reducing the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr); it is the second commonest long QT syndrome genotype.
Characteristic triggers are sudden auditory stimuli (alarm clocks, telephones, doorbells) and abrupt emotional arousal; events also occur at rest and during sleep more often than in LQT1.
The postpartum period carries a particularly high arrhythmic risk in women with LQT2, warranting planned surveillance.
The resting ECG typically shows low-amplitude, notched or bifid T waves.
The hERG channel is the molecular target of most QT-prolonging drugs, so LQT2 patients are especially vulnerable to drug-induced torsades and to hypokalaemia.
IKr is paradoxically reduced by low extracellular potassium, so maintaining potassium and correcting hypokalaemia are protective, and potassium repletion can be beneficial.
Beta-blockers reduce events but are somewhat less protective than in LQT1; minimising sudden loud alarms and startle exposure remains important.
Concealed forms with borderline resting QT exist, so genetic testing and cascade family screening add value.
reference.pathophysiology: LQT2 results from loss-of-function variants in KCNH2, which encodes the hERG (Kv11.1) subunit forming the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current, IKr, the dominant current driving phase-3 repolarisation of the ventricular action potential. Many pathogenic variants act by impairing channel trafficking, so misfolded protein is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and fails to reach the membrane, rather than by altering pore conduction alone. Reduced IKr prolongs the action potential and QT interval, increases dispersion of repolarisation and permits early afterdepolarisations that initiate torsades de pointes. IKr is unusually sensitive to extracellular potassium, so hypokalaemia further suppresses the current and heightens risk. The channel is also promiscuously blocked by numerous drugs, making hERG the principal mediator of acquired QT prolongation. Inheritance is autosomal dominant (Romano-Ward). The distinctive auditory, startle and emotional trigger profile, together with heightened postpartum risk, reflects autonomic and hormonal influences on repolarisation reserve.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital long QT subtypes, particularly LQT1 and LQT3
Acquired drug-induced QT prolongation from hERG blockade
Epilepsy misdiagnosed in place of convulsive arrhythmic syncope
Peripartum causes of collapse including postpartum cardiomyopathy
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead ECG with attention to notched or bifid, low-amplitude T-wave morphology
Ambulatory Holter and symptom-triggered event monitoring
Genetic testing including KCNH2, with cascade family screening
Review of the medication list for QT-prolonging (hERG-blocking) agents
Exercise and recovery ECG, with adrenaline provocation in selected cases
Postpartum monitoring and risk-management planning in affected women
redFlags: Syncope triggered by sudden noise (alarm clock, telephone) or intense emotion
Arrhythmic events occurring in the postpartum period
Documented torsades de pointes or aborted cardiac arrest
Family history of sudden unexplained death
Symptomatic exposure to QT-prolonging drugs or hypokalaemia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable with beta-blockade, strict avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs, maintenance of potassium and reduction of auditory and emotional triggers. The postpartum months and periods of drug or electrolyte challenge are windows of heightened arrhythmic risk.
pitfalls: Failing to anticipate and monitor the postpartum high-risk window
Tolerating hypokalaemia rather than actively correcting it
Assuming a normal resting QT excludes disease
Leaving loud alarm clocks or telephones at the bedside despite the auditory-trigger profile
references: International inherited arrhythmia / long QT syndrome consensus guidelines
management: Start beta-blockade with a non-selective agent such as nadolol or propranolol as first-line therapy and reinforce adherence
Maintain and replete potassium, since the IKr current is suppressed by hypokalaemia, and correct magnesium
Reduce startle triggers by removing alarm clocks, telephones and doorbells from the bedroom and counselling against sudden auditory stimuli
Rigorously avoid QT-prolonging hERG-blocking drugs, to which these patients are especially vulnerable
Institute planned surveillance and continued beta-blockade through the high-risk postpartum period
Treat torsades de pointes acutely with intravenous magnesium and potassium repletion, and defibrillate sustained arrhythmia or arrest
Add left cardiac sympathetic denervation or an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for recurrent events or high-risk features
Offer KCNH2 genetic testing with cascade family screening and manage through an inherited cardiac conditions service
